claim: The specialised regional functionality of the mature human cortex partly emerges through experience-dependent specialisation during early development.
source: The specialised regional functionality of the mature human cortex partly emerges through experience-dependent specialisation during early development.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain development that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Functional specialisation will be underpinned by better coordinated haemodynamic and metabolic changes in a broadly orchestrated physiological response.
source: We speculate that functional specialisation will be underpinned by better coordinated haemodynamic and metabolic changes in a broadly orchestrated physiological response.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this as speculation.

claim: Social processing is accompanied by spatially and temporally specific increases in coupled activation in the temporal-parietal junction in 4- to 7-month-old infants.
source: In 4- to 7-month-old infants, we use these new tools to show that social processing is accompanied by spatially and temporally specific increases in coupled activation in the temporal-parietal junction, a core hub region of the adult social brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: During non-social processing, coupled activation decreased in the temporal-parietal junction, indicating specificity to social processing.
source: During non-social processing, coupled activation decreased in the same region, indicating specificity to social processing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Coupling was strongest with high-frequency brain activity (beta and gamma).
source: Coupling was strongest with high-frequency brain activity (beta and gamma), consistent with the greater energetic requirements and more localised action of high-frequency brain activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: High-frequency brain activity has greater energetic requirements and more localised action.
source: Coupling was strongest with high-frequency brain activity (beta and gamma), consistent with the greater energetic requirements and more localised action of high-frequency brain activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge to explain the observed coupling pattern.

claim: Specialised functioning emerges across development through a combination of genetically influenced brain architecture and experience-expectant learning processes and experience-dependent processes.
source: This specialised functioning emerges across development through a combination of genetically influenced brain architecture and experience-expectant learning processes (generalised neural development that occurs as a result of common experiences) and experience-dependent (variation in the environment contributing to individual differences in neural response) (Johnson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson, 2001.

claim: Interactive specialisation is a theory of brain development that posits that functional specialisation emerges through competition between brain regions.
source: Interactive specialisation is a theory of brain development that posits that functional specialisation emerges through competition between brain regions (Johnson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson, 2011.

claim: Functional specialisation can be indexed as a smaller spatial extent of neural responses to a particular stimulus category and concomitant selectivity in responsive regions.
source: Thus, functional specialisation can be indexed as a smaller spatial extent of neural responses to a particular stimulus category and concomitant selectivity in responsive regions (Jones et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2015.

claim: The brain consumes 20–25% of the body's energy in adulthood while representing only 2% of the body's mass.
source: The brain is an energetically costly organ, consuming 20–25% of the body's energy in adulthood while representing only 2% of the body's mass (Raichle and Mintun, 2006; Sokoloff, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raichle and Mintun, 2006 and Sokoloff, 1999.

claim: In the first year of life, up to 60% of available energy is used by the brain.
source: There are also substantial developmental changes in the brain's energy consumption; in the first year of life, up to 60% of available energy is used by the brain (Steiner, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Steiner, 2019.

claim: When brain regions become functionally active, neurons fire more rapidly, requiring greater supplies of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
source: When brain regions become functionally active (e.g. during stimulus processing) neurons fire more rapidly, requiring greater supplies of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) (energy stores).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neural function.

claim: Producing ATP requires oxygen, and this is supplied through a localised increase in oxygenated haemoglobin in the blood.
source: Producing ATP requires oxygen, and this is supplied through a localised increase in oxygenated haemoglobin in the blood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: There are spatial dependencies between activated and deactivated regions in the adult brain.
source: Increases in oxygenated haemoglobin do not happen concurrently in all brain areas, and there are spatial dependencies between activated and deactivated regions in the adult brain (Leech et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leech et al., 2014.

claim: Energy supplies are important to synaptic plasticity, memory, and learning.
source: Energy supplies are important to synaptic plasticity, memory, and learning (Vaynman et al., 2006), and the mechanism through which energy supplies are coupled to activation (neurovascular coupling, see ) also develops through experience-dependent specialisation in the infant brain (Kozberg and Hillman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vaynman et al., 2006 and Kozberg and Hillman, 2016.

claim: Neurovascular coupling develops through experience-dependent specialisation in the infant brain.
source: Energy supplies are important to synaptic plasticity, memory, and learning (Vaynman et al., 2006), and the mechanism through which energy supplies are coupled to activation (neurovascular coupling, see ) also develops through experience-dependent specialisation in the infant brain (Kozberg and Hillman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kozberg and Hillman, 2016.

claim: Energy supply constraints may be one factor that contributes to the emergence of brain specialisation.
source: Thus, energy supply constraints may be one factor that contributes to the emergence of brain specialisation.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on inference from the preceding discussion.

claim: Core regions of the social brain (particularly the fusiform face area) show increases in oxygenated haemoglobin delivery in response to faces by 4–9 months.
source: For example, studies with fMRI indicate that core regions of the social brain (particular the fusiform face area) show increases in oxygenated haemoglobin delivery in response to faces by 4–9 months (Kosakowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kosakowski et al., 2022.

claim: Oxygenated haemoglobin delivery in response to naturalistic social videos in a broad region of temporal cortex emerges over the first hours of life.
source: Further, fNIRS studies show that oxygenated haemoglobin delivery in response to naturalistic social videos in a broad region of temporal cortex emerges over the first hours of life (Farroni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farroni et al., 2013.

claim: Developmental increases in differentiated theta power responses to social versus non-social stimuli occur between 6 and 12 months.
source: Work with EEG indicates developmental increases in differentiated theta power responses to social versus non-social stimuli between 6 and 12 months (Jones et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2015.

claim: Broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) uses a broad range of optical wavelengths which allows the measurement of the oxidation state of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme cytochrome c oxidase (CCO).
source: Broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) is a new technique that uses a broad range of optical wavelengths which allows the measurement of the oxidation state of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme cytochrome c oxidase (CCO), thereby providing a direct measure of cellular energy metabolism (Bale et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bale et al., 2016.

claim: CCO is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and serves as the terminal electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.
source: CCO is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and serves as the terminal electron acceptor in the electron transport chain (ETC).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular biology.

claim: CCO accounts for 95% of cellular oxygen metabolism.
source: It therefore accounts for 95% of cellular oxygen metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: bNIRS allows non-invasive measurement of cellular energy metabolism alongside haemodynamics/oxygenation in awake infants.
source: In this way, bNIRS allows non-invasive measurement of cellular energy metabolism alongside haemodynamics/oxygenation in awake infants.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the bNIRS technique.

claim: Social selectivity in core regions of the adult 'social brain' can be robustly detected by 4–7 months of age.
source: Work with single modalities has demonstrated that social selectivity in core regions of the adult 'social brain' can be robustly detected by 4–7 months of age (Grossmann et al., 2010; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2012; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2013; Lloyd‐Fox et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grossmann et al., 2010; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2012; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2013; Lloyd‐Fox et al., 2018.

claim: The authors previously showed the feasibility of using bNIRS in 4- to 7-month-old typically developing infants.
source: We recently showed the feasibility of using bNIRS in 4- to 7-month-old typically developing infants (Siddiqui et al., 2021) and demonstrated the presence of unique task-relevant, regionally specific functional networks where high levels of haemodynamic and metabolic coupling were observed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work, Siddiqui et al., 2021.

claim: The authors previously demonstrated the presence of unique task-relevant, regionally specific functional networks where high levels of haemodynamic and metabolic coupling were observed.
source: We recently showed the feasibility of using bNIRS in 4- to 7-month-old typically developing infants (Siddiqui et al., 2021) and demonstrated the presence of unique task-relevant, regionally specific functional networks where high levels of haemodynamic and metabolic coupling were observed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work, Siddiqui et al., 2021.

claim: Five-month-old infants (n=42) viewed naturalistic social and non-social stimuli while concurrent EEG and broadband NIRS were measured.
source: Five-month-old infants (n=42) viewed naturalistic social and non-social stimuli (Figure 1a) while we concurrently measured EEG and broadband NIRS.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure conducted in the study.

claim: Fourier transform of continuously recorded EEG data confirmed robust broadband increases in neural activity in response to social versus non-social stimuli.
source: Fourier transform of continuously recorded EEG data from 32 channels (n=35) in 1 s segments across the time course of stimulus presentation confirmed robust broadband increases in neural activity in response to social versus non-social stimuli (Figure 1b, replicating [Jones et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, replicating previous work by Jones et al., 2015.

claim: Distinct locations sensitive to social and non-social processing were revealed by haemodynamic and metabolic coupling analysis.
source: This revealed distinct locations sensitive to social (Figure 2b) and non-social (Figure 2d) processing; the topography of these locations is similar to the topography of differentiated broadband EEG activity (Figure 2a and c), particularly for haemodynamic and metabolic coupling at channels 12 and 14 and EEG theta band activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, with reference to figures showing the results.

claim: The topography of locations showing haemodynamic and metabolic coupling is similar to the topography of differentiated broadband EEG activity, particularly for channels 12 and 14 and EEG theta band activity.
source: This revealed distinct locations sensitive to social (Figure 2b) and non-social (Figure 2d) processing; the topography of these locations is similar to the topography of differentiated broadband EEG activity (Figure 2a and c), particularly for haemodynamic and metabolic coupling at channels 12 and 14 and EEG theta band activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, with reference to figures showing the results.

claim: For the social condition, bNIRS-EEG coupling was consistently observed between bNIRS channel 14 and various EEG channels positioned over the parietal and superior temporal sulcus-temporal parietal junction regions.
source: For both conditions, bNIRS-EEG coupling was consistently observed between bNIRS channel 14 and various EEG channels, which were positioned over the parietal and superior temporal sulcus-temporal parietal junction regions, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the social condition, a coupled increase in haemodynamic/metabolic activity and neural oscillatory activity was observed in the beta, gamma, and high-gamma frequency bands, primarily concentrated in the temporo-parietal region.
source: For the social condition, a coupled increase in haemodynamic/metabolic activity and neural oscillatory activity was observed in the beta, gamma, and high-gamma frequency bands, which was primarily concentrated in the temporo-parietal region (e.g. bNIRS channel 14 and EEG electrodes Pz, PO4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the social condition, a consistent pattern of coupling with neuronal activity was observed across chromophores particularly for the beta band.
source: A consistent pattern of coupling with neuronal activity was observed across chromophores particularly for the beta band.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the non-social condition, no coupling was observed between haemodynamics and neural activity (i.e. HbO2 and HHb) for the low-frequency theta and alpha frequency bands.
source: For the non-social condition, no coupling was observed between haemodynamics and neural activity (i.e. HbO2 and HHb) for the low-frequency theta and alpha frequency bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the non-social condition, a coupled increase in metabolic activity and neural activity was observed between bNIRS channel 14 and occipital and parietal EEG locations for the theta and alpha bands.
source: Meanwhile, a coupled increase in metabolic activity and neural activity was observed between bNIRS channel 14 and occipital and parietal EEG locations (O2, PO8, P10, P4 for the theta band and P10 for the alpha band).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the non-social condition, in the high-frequency beta, gamma and high-gamma bands, coupling was observed primarily for HHb and oxCCO between bNIRS channel 14 and occipital, and parietal EEG locations.
source: Moreover, in the high-frequency beta, gamma and high-gamma bands, coupling was observed primarily for HHb and oxCCO between bNIRS channel 14 and occipital, and parietal EEG locations (Oz, O2, and PO8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the non-social condition, a consistent pattern of coupling was observed between HHb and oxCCO.
source: A consistent pattern of coupling was observed between HHb and oxCCO.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Significant differences were observed between bNIRS channel 14 and Pz (with stronger association for the social condition) in the gamma frequency band for HbO2.
source: Significant differences were observed between bNIRS channel 14 and Pz (with stronger association for the social condition) in the gamma frequency band for HbO2.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data comparing social versus non-social conditions.

claim: Significant differences were observed between bNIRS channel 14 and O2 (with stronger association for the non-social condition) in the high-gamma band for oxCCO.
source: Meanwhile, significant differences were observed between bNIRS channel 14 and O2 (with stronger association for the non-social condition) in the high-gamma band for oxCCO.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data comparing social versus non-social conditions.

claim: The differential coupling between haemodynamic/metabolic activity and neural activity suggests specificity for each condition.
source: This suggests differential coupling between haemodynamic/metabolic activity and neural activity for each condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in coupling patterns.

claim: The bNIRS-EEG coupling was most consistent with the spatial extent changes in metabolic activity (CCO).
source: The results indicate that the bNIRS-EEG coupling was most consistent with the spatial extent changes in metabolic activity (CCO).
evidence: This is a finding from the image reconstruction analysis.

claim: Naturalistic social and non-social stimuli produce broad haemodynamic changes, with smaller spatial extent of locations with coupled haemodynamic and metabolic activity.
source: Confirming previous work, naturalistic social and non-social stimuli produce broad haemodynamic changes, with smaller spatial extent of locations with coupled haemodynamic and metabolic activity (Siddiqui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the study that confirms previous work by Siddiqui et al., 2021.

claim: The study replicated previously observed greater EEG responses to social versus non-social stimuli.
source: We also replicated previously observed greater EEG responses to social versus non-social stimuli (Jones et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study that replicates previous work by Jones et al., 2015.

claim: Specific locations in the parietal and temporo-parietal regions showed differential coupling between bNIRS-EEG for social and non-social stimuli, particularly for the beta and gamma band frequency bands.
source: However, examining coupling between these two phenomena uncovered a precise pattern in which specific locations in the parietal and temporo-parietal regions showed differential coupling between bNIRS-EEG for social and non-social stimuli, particularly for the beta and gamma band frequency bands, as we predicted.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The coupling analysis approach provides a more rigorous measure of functional specialisation by identifying more localised regional areas with selective coordination of neural, haemodynamic, and metabolic activity.
source: We contend that this approach identifies a more localised regional area with selective coordination of neural, haemodynamic, and metabolic activity. The increased localisation observed in our coupling analysis may indicate our approach provides a more rigorous measure of functional specialisation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Long-range functional connectivity patterns are vital for the organisation of human brain structure and function.
source: It has been hypothesised that long-range functional connectivity patterns are vital for the organisation of human brain structure and function (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: The strongest coupling was observed between temporo-parietal bNIRS channel 14 with parietal EEG locations Pz and PO4 for the social condition (for beta and gamma frequency bands).
source: The strongest coupling was observed between temporo-parietal bNIRS channel 14 with parietal EEG locations Pz and PO4 for the social condition (for beta and gamma frequency bands).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: For the non-social condition, coupling was observed between temporo-parietal bNIRS channel 14 with occipital and parietal EEG locations Oz, O2, PO8, and P10 (for theta and beta frequency bands).
source: Meanwhile, for the non-social condition, coupling was observed between temporo-parietal bNIRS channel 14 with occipital and parietal EEG locations Oz, O2, PO8, and P10 (for theta and beta frequency bands).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Task-dependent variation in coupling between neural and haemodynamic activity across frequency bands has been demonstrated in previous EEG-fMRI studies.
source: This was expected and in line with previous EEG-fMRI studies that have demonstrated task-dependent variation in coupling between neural and haemodynamic activity across frequency bands (Scheeringa et al., 2011; Scheeringa et al., 2009; Goldman et al., 2002; Yuan et al., 2010; Niessing et al., 2005; Logothetis et al., 2001; Koch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: For resting-state simultaneous fMRI and EEG, stronger coupling between the BOLD response and neural activity has been observed for the alpha band.
source: For example, for resting-state simultaneous fMRI and EEG, stronger coupling between the BOLD response and neural activity has been observed for the alpha band (Scheeringa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scheeringa et al., 2012.

claim: For cognitive tasks, stronger coupling has been observed in the gamma frequency band.
source: Meanwhile, for cognitive tasks, stronger coupling has been observed in the gamma frequency band (Kucewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kucewicz et al., 2014.

claim: Low- and high-frequency bands independently contribute to explaining BOLD variance.
source: Scheeringa et al., 2011, investigated trial-by-trial coupling of EEG and BOLD activity and found that low- and high-frequency bands independently contribute to explaining BOLD variance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scheeringa et al., 2011.

claim: Various components involved in neurovascular coupling undergo development postnatally.
source: It is well known that various components involved in neurovascular coupling undergo development postnatally, see the review by Harris et al., 2011, for a full discussion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2011.

claim: There is extensive structural change within cerebral microvasculature including growth, extension, and proliferation of new blood vessels during postnatal development.
source: Briefly, there is an extensive structural change within cerebral microvasculature including growth, extension, and proliferation of new blood vessels (Rowan and Maxwell, 1981; Norman and O'Kusky, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rowan and Maxwell, 1981 and Norman and O'Kusky, 1986.

claim: Studies have demonstrated gradual development of vascular reactivity (i.e. change in vascular tone, vasoconstriction, and vasodilation).
source: Further, studies have also demonstrated gradual development of vascular reactivity (i.e. change in vascular tone, vasoconstriction, and vasodilation) (Scheeringa et al., 2011; Scheeringa et al., 2009) which is necessary for the propagation of the NVC response (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scheeringa et al., 2011; Scheeringa et al., 2009; and Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Pericytes and astrocytes undergo development in size, number, connectivity, and branching.
source: Lastly, pericytes and astrocytes which are key components of NVC are also known to undergo development in size, number, connectivity, and branching (Kozberg and Hillman, 2016; Fujimoto, 1995; Seregi et al., 1987; Stichel et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozberg and Hillman, 2016; Fujimoto, 1995; Seregi et al., 1987; and Stichel et al., 1991.

claim: Infant PET studies demonstrate regional-specific, progressive increase in the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen consumption (CMRO2).
source: From the metabolic perspective, infant positron emission tomography (PET) studies demonstrate regional-specific, progressive increase in the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen consumption (CMRO2) (Chugani et al., 1987) while others evidence a developmental maturational change in oxidative metabolism (Kozberg and Hillman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chugani et al., 1987 and Kozberg and Hillman, 2016.

claim: In adults, oxygen consumption is more spatially localised in comparison to changes in cerebral blood flow.
source: In adults, previous research has also suggested that oxygen consumption is more spatially localised in comparison to changes in cerebral blood flow (Malonek and Grinvald, 1996) and that oxCCO has distinct spatial distributions in the brain (Phan et al., 2016; Wong-Riley et al., 1993; Hevner et al., 1995), indicating that energy metabolism may be more spatially specific.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Malonek and Grinvald, 1996; Phan et al., 2016; Wong-Riley et al., 1993; and Hevner et al., 1995.

claim: oxCCO has distinct spatial distributions in the brain.
source: In adults, previous research has also suggested that oxygen consumption is more spatially localised in comparison to changes in cerebral blood flow (Malonek and Grinvald, 1996) and that oxCCO has distinct spatial distributions in the brain (Phan et al., 2016; Wong-Riley et al., 1993; Hevner et al., 1995), indicating that energy metabolism may be more spatially specific.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Phan et al., 2016; Wong-Riley et al., 1993; and Hevner et al., 1995.

claim: Energy metabolism may be more spatially specific than cerebral blood flow.
source: In adults, previous research has also suggested that oxygen consumption is more spatially localised in comparison to changes in cerebral blood flow (Malonek and Grinvald, 1996) and that oxCCO has distinct spatial distributions in the brain (Phan et al., 2016; Wong-Riley et al., 1993; Hevner et al., 1995), indicating that energy metabolism may be more spatially specific.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research.

claim: More consistent oxCCO-EEG associations across frequency bands and stimuli with more localised (fewer long-range) associations were observed in the study.
source: In our study, we observed more consistent oxCCO-EEG associations across frequency bands and stimuli with more localised (fewer long-range) associations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: EEG profiles observed in the present study are consistent with previous studies in identifying increased gamma band activity over temporal and parieto-occipital brain regions during face processing.
source: EEG profiles observed in the present study are consistent with previous studies in identifying increased gamma band activity over temporal and parieto-occipital brain regions during face processing (Uono et al., 2017; Ghuman et al., 2014; Bayer et al., 2018; Müller-Bardorff et al., 2018; Nguyen and Cunnington, 2014; Nguyen et al., 2014; Engell and McCarthy, 2011; Bossi et al., 2020; Anaki et al., 2007; Ishai et al., 2000; Pelphrey et al., 2005; Sato et al., 2014; Zion-Golumbic et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: High-frequency neural firing is associated with localised processing.
source: High-frequency neural firing is associated with localised processing (von Stein and Sarnthein, 2000) whilst lower-frequency activity is associated with larger-scale network changes and transfer of information across systems (Canolty and Knight, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to von Stein and Sarnthein, 2000 and Canolty and Knight, 2010.

claim: Lower-frequency activity is associated with larger-scale network changes and transfer of information across systems.
source: High-frequency neural firing is associated with localised processing (von Stein and Sarnthein, 2000) whilst lower-frequency activity is associated with larger-scale network changes and transfer of information across systems (Canolty and Knight, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Canolty and Knight, 2010.

claim: The increase in lower-frequency activity during social attention may support larger-scale connectivity and communication of information through cross-frequency coupling.
source: The increase in lower-frequency activity during social attention also observed here and in other work (Jones et al., 2015; van der Velde et al., 2021) may support larger-scale connectivity and communication of information through cross-frequency coupling (Ghuman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and supported by citations to Jones et al., 2015; van der Velde et al., 2021; and Ghuman et al., 2014.

claim: Measures of metabolic load may provide important additional information in understanding localisation of brain function.
source: Our work further indicates that measures of metabolic load may provide important additional information in understanding localisation of brain function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Localised high-frequency activity exerts strong metabolic demand.
source: Localised high-frequency activity exerts strong metabolic demand (Smith et al., 2002; Kann, 2011) and subsequent increases in oxygenated haemoglobin (Logothetis et al., 2001; Niessing et al., 2005; Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2002; Kann, 2011; Logothetis et al., 2001; Niessing et al., 2005; and Goense and Logothetis, 2008.

claim: Localised high-frequency activity leads to subsequent increases in oxygenated haemoglobin.
source: Localised high-frequency activity exerts strong metabolic demand (Smith et al., 2002; Kann, 2011) and subsequent increases in oxygenated haemoglobin (Logothetis et al., 2001; Niessing et al., 2005; Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Logothetis et al., 2001; Niessing et al., 2005; and Goense and Logothetis, 2008.

claim: Increases in metabolic rate are supported by increased activity in the mitochondrial ETC, resulting in changes in CCO detected with broadband NIRS.
source: These increases in metabolic rate are supported by increased activity in the mitochondrial ETC, resulting in the changes in CCO we detected with broadband NIRS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on established knowledge.

claim: Nitric oxide and carbon dioxide are key signalling molecules in controlling neurovascular coupling and subsequent oxygen delivery.
source: Nitric oxide (which competes with oxygen to bind to CCO) and carbon dioxide (produced as a by-product in the ETC) are key signalling molecule in controlling neurovascular coupling and thus subsequent oxygen delivery (Hosford and Gourine, 2019; Hosford et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hosford and Gourine, 2019 and Hosford et al., 2022.

claim: Reactive oxygen species produced by the ETC are a key signal in inducing synaptic plasticity.
source: Finally, reactive oxygen species produced by the ETC are a key signal in inducing synaptic plasticity (Oswald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oswald et al., 2018.

claim: Social attention induces localised high-frequency brain activity in the temporal parietal junction, which increases local metabolic rates, triggering synaptic plasticity and subsequent oxygen delivery to a broader region.
source: Thus, our work is consistent with a model in which social attention induces localised high-frequency brain activity in the temporal parietal junction, which increases local metabolic rates, triggering synaptic plasticity and subsequent oxygen delivery to a broader region.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the study's findings and established knowledge.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction shows strong coupling and social selectivity.
source: Our work particularly highlights the temporal-parietal junction is showing strong coupling and social selectivity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Previous studies measuring haemodynamic activity have identified early sensitivity of the temporal-parietal junction to social stimuli from at least 4 months.
source: Previous studies measuring haemodynamic activity have identified early sensitivity of this region to social stimuli from at least 4 months (Lloyd-Fox et al., 2017), alongside a broader network of other regions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lloyd-Fox et al., 2017.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction has coupled neuronal, metabolic, and haemodynamic activity that is modulated in opposite directions by complex social and non-social content.
source: Here, we pinpoint this specific location as having coupled neuronal, metabolic, and haemodynamic activity that is modulated in opposite directions by complex social and non-social content.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: In the adult brain, the temporal-parietal junction has been linked to mentalising.
source: In the adult brain, the temporal-parietal junction has received considerable attention and there are several competing models of its function. It has been linked to mentalising (Schurz et al., 2014; Schurz et al., 2017) and reorienting attention to behaviourally relevant stimuli (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002); it can be viewed as a nexus area where the convergence of attention, language, memory, and social processing supports a social context for behaviour (Carter and Huettel, 2013) or as a region that is active when awareness of a prediction permits attentional control (Wilterson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schurz et al., 2014 and Schurz et al., 2017.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction has been linked to reorienting attention to behaviourally relevant stimuli.
source: In the adult brain, the temporal-parietal junction has received considerable attention and there are several competing models of its function. It has been linked to mentalising (Schurz et al., 2014; Schurz et al., 2017) and reorienting attention to behaviourally relevant stimuli (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002); it can be viewed as a nexus area where the convergence of attention, language, memory, and social processing supports a social context for behaviour (Carter and Huettel, 2013) or as a region that is active when awareness of a prediction permits attentional control (Wilterson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corbetta and Shulman, 2002.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction can be viewed as a nexus area where the convergence of attention, language, memory, and social processing supports a social context for behaviour.
source: In the adult brain, the temporal-parietal junction has received considerable attention and there are several competing models of its function. It has been linked to mentalising (Schurz et al., 2014; Schurz et al., 2017) and reorienting attention to behaviourally relevant stimuli (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002); it can be viewed as a nexus area where the convergence of attention, language, memory, and social processing supports a social context for behaviour (Carter and Huettel, 2013) or as a region that is active when awareness of a prediction permits attentional control (Wilterson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carter and Huettel, 2013.

claim: The temporal-parietal junction is a region that is active when awareness of a prediction permits attentional control.
source: In the adult brain, the temporal-parietal junction has received considerable attention and there are several competing models of its function.
